feedback: If the learner expects CO2 to block incoming sunlight, point them back to the model: sunlight still comes in; it is the OUTGOING infrared that is absorbed and re-radiated.

If the learner thinks a 0.04% gas cannot matter, have them vary only the CO2 control and note that a small slice still visibly moves the thermometer: separate 'how much there is' from 'how powerful it is'.
If the learner treats all greenhouse warming as bad, use the natural baseline level to show the effect keeps Earth habitable; only the enhanced effect from extra CO2 is the problem.
activities.intendedInsight: CO2 is a trace gas (~0.04%) yet climatically powerful because it absorbs and re-emits outgoing infrared; human emissions raise CO2, which raises global temperature — a cause-and-effect chain the learner generates rather than a slogan.
learnerActions: Start from the greenhouse view: watch sunlight stream onto the surface and infrared radiate back out toward space.

Move a CO2 control to thicken the atmospheric 'blanket' so more outgoing infrared is re-radiated back down, and read the thermometer as it changes; compare the natural baseline level with an enhanced (higher-CO2) level.
Read a composition pie showing CO2 as roughly 0.04% of the air, then state in your own words how such a small slice can still change the temperature you just observed.
Switch to the emissions view and raise the fossil-fuel-burning and deforestation controls; watch the atmospheric-CO2 graph rise (echoing the real Keeling curve) and a global-temperature trace follow.
Write the causal chain the model produced: burn fossil fuels / deforest → CO2 rises → more infrared trapped → global temperature rises.
activities.title: Drive a two-part climate model: greenhouse effect and emissions

feedback: For composition errors, restate ~78% N2, ~21% O2, ~1% Ar, ~0.04% CO2 and show the pie.
For a chain mis-ordering, remind that CO2 must rise before more infrared is trapped and before temperature rises.
If a consequence is missing or wrong, link higher global temperature to a concrete outcome such as rising sea levels or more frequent extreme weather.
For graph-reading errors, point to the rising CO2 (Keeling) curve and the century temperature record as the evidence base.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the facts and the chain: correct composition, which gases trap infrared, the ordered cause-and-effect, a named consequence, and interpretation of trend data.
learnerActions: Set or select the approximate percentages of N2, O2, Ar and CO2 (e.g. 78% / 21% / ~1% / ~0.04%).
Choose which gases are greenhouse gases and which are not.
Put the causal chain in order: burn fossil fuels → CO2 rises → more infrared trapped → temperature rises.
Identify one specific consequence of climate change (e.g. rising sea levels, more extreme weather).
Read a CO2/temperature graph and state what the trend shows and why it matters.
activities.title: Checkpoint: composition, mechanism, causal chain, consequence and graph reading
